title: Movie Robots vs Real Robots
tagline: Could the robots from the films actually exist? What's real, what's still fiction.
description: Ten short, fact-checked lessons that take famous robots from films — the Terminator, WALL-E, R2-D2, C-3PO, androids and more — and compare them to what real robotics can and can't do today.
outcome: After this course you can explain, with real numbers and examples, which parts of famous movie robots are realistic and which are still science fiction.
whoFor: Anyone who has watched a robot movie and wondered 'could that actually happen?' — no robotics background needed.
prerequisites: None. No maths or coding needed.
outcomes: Explain why a Terminator-style power source is not realistic with today's batteries
Describe what real rolling utility and translation robots can actually do
Explain why Asimov's Three Laws are hard to turn into real code
Describe what makes androids and bionic limbs realistic, and what's still missing
Trace the idea of lifelike machines from 1700s clockwork to today's animatronics and robot pets

finalActivity.title: Pick one movie robot and fact-check it
finalActivity.prompt: Pick one robot from a film you know. Write one sentence on what part of it is realistic today, and one sentence on what part is still science fiction, and why.

lessons.title: Could a Terminator Really Exist?
lessons.summary: Work out, with real battery numbers, why a self-powered humanoid like the T-800 is science fiction.

quiz.q: Today's best humanoid robot batteries last for about how long at peak performance?
options: About 5 hours
About 5 days
About 5 months
quiz.why: Figure AI's F.03 battery gives roughly 5 hours at peak output — real batteries, not movie ones.

quiz.q: Why can't a small battery run a robot for decades, as films sometimes suggest?
options: Batteries are illegal above a certain size
Energy storage per kilogram is far below what that much runtime needs
Robots are not allowed to run unattended
quiz.why: Lithium-ion stores far less energy per kilogram than a power cell would need to run a human-sized robot for years.

quiz.q: Comparing energy density, lithium-ion batteries store roughly how much less energy per kilogram than gasoline?
options: About the same
Around 2 times less
Around 50 times less
quiz.why: Gasoline packs roughly 50 times more energy per kilogram than lithium-ion, which is why liquid fuel still beats batteries for long, heavy-duty runtimes.

quiz.q: What is the biggest real engineering barrier to a Terminator-style robot, more than appearance?
options: Finding the right paint colour
Power, actuators and control working together at human-like performance for a long time
Making a voice chip
quiz.why: Looking humanoid is the easy part; sustaining human-level strength, dexterity and endurance on a portable power source is the hard, unsolved part.

lessons.title: Could a Real WALL-E Clean Up Earth?
lessons.summary: Compare WALL-E's one-robot-does-everything story with how real cleanup and compaction robots actually work.

quiz.q: Real-world waste robots today mostly do what, compared to WALL-E?
options: One narrow job each, like sorting recyclables
Every waste job a planet needs, alone
Nothing yet — no waste robots exist
quiz.why: Today's waste-handling robots are specialists (sorting, compacting, hauling) rather than one generalist like WALL-E.

quiz.q: What makes compacting trash into a cube, like WALL-E does, mechanically demanding?
options: It needs very little force
It needs sustained high force and durable parts to survive constant wear
It only works on paper
quiz.why: Repeated heavy compaction is hard on motors and structure, which is why real compactors are big fixed machines, not small mobile robots.

quiz.q: Why would cleaning up a whole planet's waste need more than one robot design?
options: Waste types and terrain vary too much for one machine to handle well
All waste looks the same everywhere
Robots cannot sort materials
quiz.why: Different waste (organic, plastic, electronic) and different terrain each suit different specialised machines, not a single do-everything robot.

quiz.q: What's a realistic version of 'WALL-E's job' happening today?
options: Nothing comparable exists
Fleets of specialised sorting and recycling robots in waste facilities
A single robot that already cleans entire cities alone
quiz.why: Modern recycling centres already use robotic arms and sorting systems — just as a fleet of specialists, not one generalist.

lessons.title: Could a Robot Like R2-D2 Really Exist?
lessons.summary: Check R2-D2's rolling, tool-arm, translator abilities against what wheeled utility robots can really do.

quiz.q: Which part of R2-D2 is closest to robots that already exist?
options: Rolling with tool arms for a specific job
Faster-than-light travel
Reading minds
quiz.why: Small wheeled utility robots with extending tool arms already exist for maintenance and inspection work.

quiz.q: Why is R2-D2's instant translation of every language still unrealistic for a small onboard robot?
options: Translation needs huge processing power and data most small robots don't carry
Robots cannot make sounds
There is only one spoken language on Earth
quiz.why: Broad real-time translation today typically relies on large models and heavy compute, usually run in the cloud, not squeezed into a small astromech-sized unit.

quiz.q: What would be the hardest part of giving a real robot R2-D2's range of tools?
options: Nothing — tools are simple to add
Packing many different actuators and power into a small body without it becoming too heavy or fragile
Tools are banned by robotics safety rules
quiz.why: Every added tool needs its own actuator, wiring and power draw, which quickly adds size and weight to a small body.

quiz.q: A real rolling utility robot like R2-D2 would most likely be used for…
options: Inspecting equipment and carrying tools in tight spaces
Replacing human pilots unsupervised
Nothing; wheels can't be useful in the field
quiz.why: Compact wheeled robots are good at exactly this: moving through tight spaces to inspect or carry things.

lessons.title: C-3PO: Can a Robot Understand Every Language?
lessons.summary: Look at how real translation AI works, and why 'fluent in six million forms of communication' is still fiction.

quiz.q: Modern translation AI mostly learns language from…
options: Huge amounts of text and speech data
A single rulebook written by one person
Guessing randomly until it's right
quiz.why: Today's translation systems are trained on massive datasets of real language examples, not hand-written rules.

quiz.q: Why do translation systems still struggle with some languages?
options: Those languages have far less training data available
All languages are equally easy for computers
It is impossible to translate any language with AI
quiz.why: Less-documented languages have less data to train on, so accuracy is uneven across languages.

quiz.q: What is still missing compared to C-3PO's fluent understanding of any form of communication?
options: Robust, instant understanding of truly novel or invented communication forms
Any translation ability at all
The ability to speak any words out loud
quiz.why: Real systems are strong on known human languages but not on inventing understanding for entirely unknown communication, which is where fiction goes further.

quiz.q: Why is 'six million forms of communication' an exaggeration for any real system?
options: No database or model currently holds that much distinct linguistic coverage with high accuracy
Six million is actually too small a number
All languages are identical in structure
quiz.why: Maintaining high-quality understanding across millions of distinct forms is far beyond today's coverage, which focuses on a few hundred major languages well.

lessons.title: Asimov's Three Laws: Why They Don't Work in Real Life
lessons.summary: Walk through the Three Laws of Robotics and the real-world loophole that breaks the First Law.

quiz.q: Asimov's First Law says a robot may not injure a human or, through inaction, allow…
options: A human to come to harm
A robot to be damaged
A door to stay open
quiz.why: The First Law combines both: no direct harm, and no harm through standing by and doing nothing.

quiz.q: Why do real engineers find the Three Laws hard to actually programme?
options: 'Harm' and 'human' are not simple, clearly measurable things for software to judge in every situation
The laws are too short to type into code
Robots cannot follow any instructions
quiz.why: Turning a vague concept like 'harm' into precise, reliable code that holds up in every real situation is an unsolved problem.

quiz.q: What's an example of a conflict that breaks a strict reading of the First Law?
options: Two humans need conflicting help at once, and the robot cannot fully satisfy both
A robot refuses to move at all
A robot only works on sunny days
quiz.why: When helping one person risks or limits help to another, a simple rule can't resolve the trade-off cleanly.

quiz.q: What do real robot safety systems use instead of Asimov's three sentences?
options: Detailed engineering standards, sensors, and specific rules for specific situations
Nothing; real robots have no safety rules
A single moral statement memorised by the robot
quiz.why: Real-world safety relies on concrete engineering standards and situational rules, not one elegant universal law.

lessons.title: Androids: How Close Are We to Robots That Look Human?
lessons.summary: See what today's most human-looking androids can and can't do, and why faces are the hardest part.

quiz.q: What is typically the hardest part of making an android look convincingly human?
options: The face and its subtle expressions
The legs
The paint colour
quiz.why: Human faces carry huge subtlety in micro-expressions that are extremely hard to replicate convincingly with motors and skin.

quiz.q: What does 'uncanny valley' describe?
options: The discomfort people feel when something looks almost, but not quite, human
A place where robots are built
A type of robot motor
quiz.why: The uncanny valley is the dip in comfort when a robot is close to human-looking but something feels subtly wrong.

quiz.q: Today's most advanced androids are mainly used for…
options: Research, demonstrations and limited public interaction
Replacing all human jobs
Flying planes
quiz.why: Current androids are impressive demonstrations and research platforms, not yet general-purpose workers.

quiz.q: Why do many functional humanoid robots (not androids) skip a human-like face entirely?
options: A simple or no face avoids uncanny valley discomfort and is cheaper to build
Faces are against safety regulations
Faces make robots heavier than anything else on the body
quiz.why: Skipping a detailed face sidesteps the uncanny valley problem and simplifies the build, which is why many humanoids have simple screens or no face.

lessons.title: Cyborgs and Bionic Limbs: Real People with Robot Parts
lessons.summary: Meet the real bionic limbs and implants people use today, and what they can and can't feel.

quiz.q: A modern bionic hand mainly reads control signals from…
options: The user's remaining muscle or nerve signals
A keyboard the user types on
Random motion
quiz.why: Bionic limbs typically pick up electrical signals from the wearer's own muscles or nerves to decide how to move.

quiz.q: Can current advanced bionic hands give the wearer a sense of touch?
options: Some can provide limited feedback like pressure or texture cues
They give full human-level touch sensation
They give no feedback of any kind, ever
quiz.why: Some advanced prosthetics provide limited sensory feedback, but it's far from the full range of human touch.

quiz.q: What is a cyborg, in the everyday sense used in this video?
options: A person whose body is combined with technology, like an implant or bionic limb
A robot that looks exactly like a person
A fictional-only concept with no real examples
quiz.why: In common usage, a cyborg is simply a person integrated with technology — a real and already-existing category, unlike a fully fictional android.

quiz.q: What is a major ongoing challenge for bionic limbs?
options: Making control natural, comfortable and durable for daily life
Finding any material light enough to use
Legal bans on all prosthetics
quiz.why: Getting a limb to feel natural, last through daily wear, and respond accurately is still an active area of engineering.

lessons.title: The Clockwork Robots of the 1700s
lessons.summary: Discover the mechanical automatons that wrote, drew and played music centuries before electronics existed.

quiz.q: What powered the automatons of the 1700s, since there was no electricity?
options: Wound-up springs and gears, like a clock
Batteries
Steam engines the size of houses
quiz.why: These automatons used clockwork mechanisms — springs and precisely cut gears — just like mechanical clocks of the era.

quiz.q: What could the famous 'Writer' automaton actually do?
options: Dip a pen and write a pre-set message by hand
Understand language and compose new sentences
Speak out loud
quiz.why: The Writer followed a fixed mechanical program encoded in cams to trace out specific letters — impressive mimicry, not understanding.

quiz.q: Why do these clockwork automatons matter to robotics history?
options: They show that the idea of a machine performing lifelike actions is centuries old
They were the first robots to use computer chips
They proved electricity was unnecessary forever
quiz.why: They demonstrate that the dream of lifelike automated machines long predates electronics and computing.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between a clockwork automaton and a modern robot?
options: A modern robot can sense its environment and adjust; a clockwork automaton just repeats a fixed mechanical sequence
Automatons are always bigger
There is no real difference
quiz.why: Automatons replay one fixed sequence with no sensing or feedback; modern robots can sense and adapt.

lessons.title: How Theme-Park Animatronics Move
lessons.summary: Look under the skin of a theme-park animatronic figure: the hidden motors, air cylinders and show control system.

quiz.q: Many theme-park animatronics get quick, powerful motion from…
options: Compressed air (pneumatics) rather than only electric motors
Magic
Nothing; they don't actually move
quiz.why: Pneumatic actuators give the fast, strong bursts of motion often seen in animatronic figures.

quiz.q: What runs the precise timing between an animatronic's movements and its audio?
options: A show control system synchronising pre-programmed cues
Nothing; it's all improvised live
A human puppeteer manually timing every move
quiz.why: Show control systems cue motion, lights and sound together on a precise programmed timeline.

quiz.q: Why do animatronics not need true intelligence to seem lifelike?
options: They replay a carefully designed fixed show, not open-ended decisions
They secretly contain a human operator every time
They are not actually controlled at all
quiz.why: A well-designed repeating show can look convincingly lifelike without any real-time decision-making.

quiz.q: What's a key design goal for animatronic figures beyond movement?
options: Reliability — working correctly thousands of times a day for guests
Being as heavy as possible
Avoiding any kind of show timing
quiz.why: Theme parks need figures to perform reliably show after show, all day, every day.

lessons.title: Robot Pets: Can a Machine Be a Friend?
lessons.summary: From Aibo to modern companion robots, see what robot pets actually sense, and what 'companionship' means here.

quiz.q: What do robot pets like Aibo use to seem responsive to their owner?
options: Sensors like touch, sound and cameras paired with programmed behaviours
Nothing; they move completely at random
A live human controlling them remotely
quiz.why: Robot pets combine sensors with programmed responses to react in ways that feel attentive.

quiz.q: Why might a robot pet help some people, such as those in care homes?
options: It can offer a sense of companionship and routine without the demands of a living animal
It can fully replace human relationships
It requires no care or charging at all
quiz.why: Robot pets are used in some care settings to offer comfort and routine without the responsibilities of a live animal — a real, documented use case.

quiz.q: What's a key limitation of a robot pet's 'emotions'?
options: They are simulated behaviours, not genuine feelings
They are identical to human emotions
They make the robot legally a living being
quiz.why: A robot pet's reactions are designed behaviours triggered by sensors, not subjective feelings.

quiz.q: How has robot pet technology changed since early models like Aibo?
options: Newer models use better sensors and AI for more natural-feeling responses
It has not changed at all since the 1990s
Robot pets have been discontinued entirely
quiz.why: Sensor and AI improvements have made companion robots noticeably more responsive over time.
